positive: Many viewers are eager and impatient for pre-orders to open, with some planning to order the moment they can, regardless of price.
Commenters often name their intended configuration, mostly white with large storage and unlocked, citing storage needs or a wish for a non-black phone.
Some admit they don't truly need it but feel drawn to it, and even past foldable skeptics say they will order.
Many commenters say they are excited and plan to buy or preorder the Duo as soon as it is released.
Viewers who wanted a foldable phone but did not want to leave iOS see this as the device they have been waiting for.
Some accept missing features or a weaker camera, preferring a large pocketable screen and a new kind of Apple device from day one.
negative: Many commenters say the price is far too high, joking that buying the phone would cost a fortune or empty their wallet.
Some plan to wait for a later version or for proof the foldable screen holds up without creasing or breaking.
Others mock the name and marketing, and criticise Apple and its loyal buyers for overhyping ordinary features.

positive: Most commenters say they plan to buy the phone anyway, so the 'reasons not to buy' points rarely persuade them.
The drawbacks people name are minor to them: Touch ID instead of Face ID and no telephoto lens. Some even like Touch ID.
The high price, about 3,000 in Canada, comes up, but interest-free financing and free AppleCare offers make it seem manageable.
negative: Price is the main objection: commenters see the phone as too expensive, with higher storage tiers and tax pushing the total even further.
Some see it as a copycat of existing foldables, and say Android phones are better for cameras.
Some features, such as built-in MagSafe, are seen as pointless since most people use a case, and storage adds little trade-in value.

positive: Many commenters say the design, folding transition and software polish impress them, and some say Apple's version finally won them over to foldables.
Some see the price as justified or acceptable, for example because the phone replaces two devices or offers useful multitasking, though a few admit cost is a concern or out of reach.
Several value practical uses such as reading documents, a smaller folded size and big storage, and care little about camera quality.
negative: Many commenters see the roughly $2,000 starting price as excessive, comparing it to rent or multiple devices, especially given current economic pressures.
Several say the price isn't justified because Apple cut features such as water resistance and offers modest base storage.
Some worry about costly repairs and durability from the folding design, and say the price makes them unwilling to buy despite interest.

positive: Many commenters on older phones, such as the 12, 13, 14 and 15 Pro models, plan to upgrade to the Duo, often using trade-ins to offset the price.
Several prefer the Duo because the Pro line feels unchanged year to year, while the Duo offers a new experience and a bigger screen.
negative: Many commenters say the Duo's price is too high, especially for a device they see as a downgrade from a Pro Max.
Camera compromises, such as a weaker main lens and less zoom, and the lack of Face ID are common deal-breakers.
Several are choosing the 18 Pro Max, often with a tablet, or waiting for a later Duo version with fewer unknowns.

positive: Many commenters who own a Samsung Fold say they are happy with it, praising its thinness, light weight, customisation and comfort with the crease.
Several longtime Samsung users admit they are surprised and impressed by Apple's first foldable, while others say Apple's late entry usually brings refinement and ecosystem strength.
Some defend Samsung as the innovator and say Apple's entry should push it to bring back features like stylus support and water resistance.
negative: Many commenters say Apple is late to foldables and presents as new an idea Samsung and others have offered for years.
Several complain the Duo is too expensive, and some say it costs more than Samsung's Fold models and should have top cameras.
Some compare specs and trade-offs: the Duo is heavier than Samsung's Fold, and each brand has drawbacks such as software, buttons, and durability ratings.

positive: Many commenters praise Apple's polished software, animations and fold transition, saying it feels distinctively Apple and is impressive for a first foldable.
Existing Apple users say they waited for an Apple foldable instead of buying Android ones, citing the ecosystem, iOS simplicity and trust in build quality.
Some say Apple succeeds by refining others' ideas, and that borrowing between companies benefits consumers, though a few note Android rivals offer features or hardware first.
negative: Many commenters say Apple lacks original ideas, copies Android and Samsung features, and arrives years late with foldables and other tech.
Apple fans are accused of hypocrisy: they dismissed foldables as gimmicks before Apple made one, and now praise or want them.
Others criticise Apple's pricing, first-generation reliability, and mediocre hardware, though a few defend its polish or ask about repair access.

positive: Many commenters praise the matte inner screen, saying it looks attractive, helps hide the crease, and suits long reading sessions.
The transition between the outer screen and the unfolded display is widely described as smooth, clean and impressive.
Commenters value the larger pocketable screen for multitasking and readable text, and some are impressed the crease is barely noticeable.
negative: Many dislike the inner screen's matte, anti-reflective finish and curved edges, and see it as a way to hide the crease. They also feel Apple plays down the crease and hinge.
Commenters worry about durability and repair costs: foldable screens failing after about a year, expensive replacements, possible high AppleCare deductibles, and costly protectors and accessories.
Others criticise the display setup: the small front screen is awkward for everyday use, and the inner screen looks less sharp. They also say the extra size isn't worth the price.

positive: Many commenters prefer a hidden under-display camera to a punch-hole or permanent cutout, valuing an uninterrupted, clean full screen.
Some argue selfies would mostly use the outer display camera anyway, so the inner camera's quality matters less to average users.
The matte inner display is praised for helping hide the crease and giving the foldable a smooth, appealing look.
negative: Several commenters say under-display cameras have poor image quality and were abandoned for that reason, though some don't care since they rarely take selfies.
Complaints about the inner screen: grainy look, inaccurate colors, and fingerprint grease showing up often, with mixed feelings about the matte finish.
Some dislike protruding rear camera bumps that stop the phone lying flat, and a few want more rear lenses.

positive: Commenters widely praise the open and close transition as smooth, clean and seamless, with many calling it genius or a standout feature.
Several credit the design team and say the animation alone could drive sales, even winning over fans of rival brands.
Some like the blur and see-through glass effect, saying it makes the fold feel natural and very Apple-like.
negative: Commenters are unimpressed that an opening and closing animation is treated as a headline feature, seeing it as a sign the phone lacks stronger selling points.
Some downplay the effect as a simple blur transition, not especially impressive or innovative.
One commenter noted the animation glitched when closing the device.

positive: Some think the concern is exaggerated, suggesting a software setting could flip the layout for left-handed users.
negative: Left-handed users say the dual-screen layout seems designed for right-handed use and would feel awkward or unusable for them.
Some commenters are put off by Face ID placement, saying unlocking would be frustrating for left-handers and they would wait for a redesign.
Several comments sarcastically echo a 'holding it wrong' response, implying the maker dismisses left-handed people's concerns.

positive: Pencil support is a major selling point for some viewers, who see the inner screen as a mini iPad for productivity.
Several people want to sketch and paint on the phone and hope apps like Procreate add support.
Some Android foldable owners say the lack of pen support on their devices makes Apple's option more appealing.
Many see the foldable as a combined iPhone and iPad mini, and some plan to replace both devices with one pocketable unit.

Commenters praise the form factor and software, including the side toolbar, flexible orientations, and sensible button placement, and see uses such as reading, navigation, medical work and retro gaming.
Several say the camera compromises don't bother them, since they mostly browse and watch media or use a separate camera.
negative: Many see the foldable as essentially a pricey iPad mini in phone form, and say buying a regular iPad would make more sense.
The price is a major complaint: commenters call it poor value, a gimmick or niche device, and think early buyers should wait for later generations.
Doubts about practicality: the folded shape seems wide, people may mostly use the small outer screen, and the crease and camera setup draw criticism.

positive: Many commenters are excited about the foldable design, calling it the most interesting iPhone in years and comparing it to landmark models like the original and the iPhone X.
Several want to buy it, including long-time Apple users, some Android users, and people moving away from the older, plainer iPhone look.
Some comments praise build and display details, such as a durable titanium body, slim bezels, and a hidden front camera, and hope for a tougher screen glass.
negative: Many commenters say the foldable is very heavy, and that adding a case would make one-handed use difficult.
Some joke that Apple will advertise small improvements next year, such as a lighter body or a less visible crease.
Several see the design as copying rivals' foldables, or say Apple is behind, and that a flip style would have been better.

positive: Many commenters are very excited and plan to buy or preorder the Duo, often saying desire comes first and justification later.
People like the book-like opening, the hardware and software integration, and the design touches that reduce fold visibility and hide the selfie camera.
Commenters see it as versatile for reading, video and side-by-side scrolling, and some hope future models bring further improvements, though a few note rivals offer more specs.
negative: Many see the Duo as overpriced, with high starting costs and steep regional markups, plus carrier deals that require long commitments.
Commenters criticise the hardware: heavy and thick, a weaker camera than Pro models, an uneven camera bump, and doubts about durability and case options.
Several say rival foldables match or beat it in features or performance, and question whether Apple users want a foldable at all.

positive: Commenters like that developers, including big names such as Netflix, are adapting apps for the device, which they expect to improve app quality and even iPad versions.
The software transitions and polished design are praised, and some say the hype has made them more open to foldables.
Running two apps side by side is seen as a sensible limit, and the unfolded layout is liked for reading.
negative: Commenters doubt the multitasking features add real value, seeing the device as hype aimed at wealthy buyers rather than something people need.
Several say the app-dragging and window-arranging features feel borrowed from iPadOS, and that portrait multitasking looks limited to pop-up video.
Button placement draws complaints: the mute switch seems to be replaced by a customizable button, and volume controls sit in an awkward spot.

positive: Several commenters prefer a fingerprint sensor, saying it is faster and more reliable than Face ID and doesn't require an Apple Watch as a workaround.
Some feel more comfortable with fingerprint unlocking because it avoids constant face scanning, which they see as a privacy concern.
Other comments are broadly favourable, calling the device polished and high-tech and saying it raises their interest in buying one.
negative: Some viewers are put off by the lack of Face ID, and a missing triple camera, and say they will wait for later models.
Several comments say the device is a late, derivative take on Samsung's foldables and shows little real Apple innovation.
Others criticise the software layout, such as wasted screen space and an oversized keyboard, and say the high price is hard to justify.

positive: Many commenters see the device as polished and impressive for a first-generation foldable, and several say they plan to buy it.
Some defend the missing features, arguing Apple leaves room for later upgrades and that early shortcomings or a barely visible crease don't bother them.
A few note that other brands, such as Motorola, made foldables first, while some express excitement about Apple's first flip-style iPhone.
negative: Commenters mock Apple's foldable as late to the market, arguing that rivals already offer foldables and Apple is presenting it as a breakthrough.
Some worry about durability, especially a screen crease that may become more visible with use, as with earlier foldables they owned.
Others are suspicious of Apple's tactics, suggesting leaks about price and low supply pressure people to preorder, and noting the short return window.
